title: Flowers that fade
hookLine: a traditional offering verse: these flowers fade, and so will this body

lines: A VERSE YOU'D NEVER WRITE ON A CARD.
cards: Roses on an anniversary. A bouquet at a wedding. Plastic flowers, even, so they never droop.
Gift flowers tend to say forever. The freshest ones get picked, and when they start to brown they go out with the trash, quickly, a little embarrassed, as if the flowers had failed.

Buddhist temples are full of flowers too: jasmine, lotus, frangipani, marigolds, heaped in front of the Buddha. But there's a verse people chant while offering them, and it says something you'd never write on a card.

teach.b: The Theravada flower offering is a short Pali chant. It begins with the flowers themselves: full of color, full of fragrance, offered at the feet of the Buddha. Then it turns.

teach.h: AS THESE FADE, SO WILL THIS BODY.
teach.b: In substance it says: just as these flowers will wither, so my body will go to destruction. Try saying that while holding a fresh bunch of jasmine. It's not meant to be gloomy, though.
It's honest. The flowers are chosen precisely because they're fresh, and precisely because they won't last.
That's anicca, impermanence: everything that arises passes away. The flower shows it in a few days; the body, over a lifetime. The Dhammapada uses flowers the same way.

teach.h: THE FLOOD AND THE SLEEPING VILLAGE.
teach.b: In Max Muller's translation: "Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers, and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village."
Someone so busy picking pleasures they don't notice the water rising. The offering reverses that. You pick a flower, and you notice.
What does noticing do? Some teachers say it makes things more precious, not less. Jasmine that will be brown by Thursday is worth smelling today.

A face across the dinner table, remembered as not forever, can be looked at a little longer. So the verse isn't asking you to be sad about fading. It's asking you to be awake while the flower is fresh.
Buddhists offer flowers as respect for the Buddha, and as a mirror.
The flowers are fresh today. That is exactly why they're beautiful.

how: Theravada Buddhists offer fresh flowers at shrines and temples while chanting a short Pali verse that reflects that, as the flowers wither, so will the body.

o: a flower, offered at a shrine
a bowl of water at a shrine

games.q: match the piece of today's teaching.
p: as these fade, so will this body
makes things more precious, not less

s: the flower-offering verse is meant to make people sad
it's honest about fading so people wake up while the flower is fresh.
flowers are offered partly because they won't last
they're a mirror for impermanence, anicca.
the Dhammapada compares a distracted person to someone gathering flowers as a flood comes
death carries them off like a flood carries off a sleeping village.

games.q: you're at a Theravada temple with a bunch of fresh jasmine. what does the offering verse say?
o: as these flowers wither, so will this body.
games.why: the Pali offering verse turns from the flowers' beauty to impermanence: as they fade, so will the body.

practice: If you have a flower, a leaf, or even a picture of one, set it in front of you and look closely for a few breaths: the color, the edges, where it's already starting to change. Then feel your own hands, warm, alive, also changing.
Let each breath come and go, arising and passing, fresh and then gone; there's nothing to fix.

wordCard.voice: Puppha. Flower: the offering verse, as these flowers will wither, so will this body, and so this moment is worth waking up for.

orig.note: Pali: flower; the flower offering is puppha-puja.

carryVoice: Your line: fresh today, gone tomorrow. A flower can fade in its own time. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Flower offering chant (Pupphapuja), Theravada chanting tradition
